node-1.label: A 33-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and dyspnea on exertion, and appeared lethargic on examination

node-2.label: Patient is a 33-year-old man with no medical history; he received the Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccination approximately 4 weeks before presentation

node-3.label: Initial vitals: temperature 98.9°F, heart rate 76 beats/min, blood pressure 90/55 mm Hg, SpO₂ 99% on room air; physical examination showed a lethargic man with unremarkable cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations and no lymphadenopathy

node-4.label: Patient developed a low-grade fever of 100°F on day 1

node-5.label: Patient denied orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, sore throat, runny nose, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, night sweats, and recent tuberculosis contact

why.why: Both expert analyses reaffirm VITT/TTS as the leading diagnosis based on recent J&J vaccination, fever without infectious symptoms, abdominal pain, hypotension, and lethargy. All confirmatory results remain pending after three retrieval attempts, so definitive confirmation is still lacking; confidence is increased modestly from 0.60 to 0.65.

Exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, and vaccine-related thrombotic risk keep pulmonary embolism/infarction a secondary consideration. Expert analyses note that CT angiography is still needed and VITT/TTS cannot be definitively distinguished from PE, so confidence remains 0.25 pending imaging.

The radiologist notes that sepsis is not fully excluded, so acute infection/sepsis remains a possible alternative. However, the absence of localizing infectious symptoms and the expert consensus favoring VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis keep this unlikely; confidence is increased minimally from 0.10 to 0.12.

Abdominal pain with hypotension/lethargy in a prothrombotic post-vaccine setting supports possible splanchnic ischemia, and expert analyses indicate it cannot be excluded without abdominal CT. However, the overall clinical picture favors VITT/TTS, so confidence remains low at 0.15.

node-10.label: Expert analyses recommend contrast-enhanced CT/abdominal CT to evaluate for thrombosis and adrenal hemorrhage

node-11.label: VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis and/or adrenal hemorrhage

why.why: This broader hypothesis includes the splanchnic vein thrombosis component now identified as the leading complication by both experts; the adrenal hemorrhage component is less favored by current analyses but remains possible pending contrast-enhanced CT. Confidence is raised from 0.30 to 0.55 because the leading splanchnic vein thrombosis component is strongly supported.

node-12.label: VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis

why.why: Both experts identify VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis as the leading hypothesis, and this complication best explains the abdominal pain and hemodynamic compromise. However, anti-PF4 ELISA, serotonin release assay, and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT remain pending, and the radiologist notes that sepsis or thrombotic microangiopathy are not fully excluded; confidence is raised from 0.45 to 0.55.

attrs.why: This refines the VITT/TTS frontier to a specific cardiopulmonary complication. Hemoptysis and exertional dyspnea in a prothrombotic post-vaccine setting support pulmonary embolism, and node-7 remains a secondary consideration; under the leading VITT/TTS framework, PE/infarction is a plausible complication requiring CT angiography.

why.why: The latest expert analyses emphasize splanchnic vein thrombosis rather than adrenal hemorrhage as the leading VITT/TTS complication, and no new evidence specifically supports adrenal hemorrhage. Abdominal pain with hypotension could still be explained by adrenal hemorrhage, so it remains a low-probability consideration pending CT; confidence is reduced from 0.20 to 0.15.

node-15.label: VITT/TTS complicated by cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

attrs.why: CVST is a well-known VITT/TTS complication and could contribute to lethargy, even though headache and focal neurologic deficits are absent. This candidate refines the VITT/TTS frontier and should remain a low-probability consideration until brain imaging is obtained.

node-16.label: VITT/TTS with isolated thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy without detectable thrombosis

attrs.why: This candidate refines VITT/TTS to a thrombotic-microangiopathic state without a defined thrombus. Fever without infectious symptoms and expert recommendation for platelet/coagulation studies fit this possibility, but it is less able than other candidates to explain the focal abdominal and pulmonary symptoms, so confidence is low.

node-17.label: Anti-PF4 ELISA, serotonin release assay, platelet count, D-dimer, fibrinogen, and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT have been requested to evaluate VITT/TTS

node-18.label: Actual results of platelet count, D-dimer, fibrinogen, anti-PF4 ELISA, serotonin release assay, and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT remain unavailable despite retrieval attempts

node-19.label: Radiologist and laboratory physician analyses both identify VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis as the leading hypothesis

node-20.label: Laboratory physician reports all confirmatory results remain pending after three retrieval attempts

node-21.label: Radiologist notes that sepsis and thrombotic microangiopathy are not fully excluded

attrs.why: The radiologist explicitly states that thrombotic microangiopathy is not fully excluded. TMA can cause fever, abdominal pain, hypotension, and lethargy, and the requested platelet count and coagulation studies are still pending. However, the clinical picture is more consistent with VITT/TTS complicated by splanchnic vein thrombosis, so confidence remains low at 0.10.
